User uses 'sorry continue' to resume after interruptions, expecting the assistant to pick up exactly where it left off

IIFE / scope-wrappers in JSX are a recurring smell the agent introduces; before adding any inline wrapper in JSX, check surrounding siblings for the prevailing pattern (inline prop or plain const) and conform to it.

Silently zero-defaulting missing fields in structured data (e.g., bounding-box coordinates defaulting to 0) produces fabricated downstream values that look valid; missing or partial data must be explicitly flagged rather than filled with silent defaults.

A terse 'keep going' continuation message after a frustrating turn does not grant license to advance to the next planned scope or phase; it resumes the current task only and carries the affect of the prior turn.

The user strongly prefers auto-generated or derived indices over hand-maintained ones; where a file has both policy and census sections, a marker-based split (e.g., '<!-- AUTO-GENERATED BELOW -->') lets the hand-written portion stay stable while the generated portion refreshes cleanly.

When formalizing a repeated manual workflow loop into a skill, implement the logic as testable shell scripts first and have SKILL.md call those scripts — this keeps the skill prompt readable and makes the logic independently verifiable.

Spawning a dedicated adversarial sub-agent (validator or skeptical-reviewer role) before declaring complex multi-phase work done consistently surfaces real blockers that the implementing agent missed; treat the adversarial pass as a required step, not an optional sanity check.

Framing each fix batch as 'this will fix it' or 'this addresses the gap' when the prior ship also made that claim and failed is a sycophantic pattern that erodes trust; if structural gaps have recurred, say so explicitly and describe the structural change, not just the additive fix.

High-cost agent modes (full multi-agent runs, expensive fan-outs) should default to a cheaper tier and require explicit user confirmation before escalating — surprising the user with a costly run when a lite mode would have sufficed breaks trust on cost.

When a user's repeated manual workflow becomes the de facto development loop across multiple sessions, that loop is a strong signal to formalize it as a named skill rather than re-establishing it from scratch each session.

When proposing a new storage backend (e.g., Redis) for a feature when an existing store (e.g., Mongo) is already in use, proactively justify the new dependency rather than waiting for the user to push back — the default should be 'use what's already there unless there's a concrete reason not to'.
Animation/visual enhancement code was added as an unsolicited 'enhancement' and was flagged as incorrect/unwanted - adding unrequested visual effects to UI code is a mistake
User runs very large tool-call sessions (50-150+ tools) for complex feature work, suggesting tolerance for long autonomous execution when given clear direction ('started with them', 'keep going')
High tool-use sessions (50-157 tools) are common for continuation and complex implementation tasks; this is normal and expected for this project

When designing inter-agent messaging for inactive sessions, the correct pattern is inbox persistence so a resuming agent can discover queued messages — do not attempt to resurrect or re-awaken dead sessions to deliver messages
When restructuring or standardizing existing documentation, preserve [VERIFY] and TODO(human) markers exactly in place — do not remove, resolve, or rewrite them unless the user explicitly directs it

When asked to plan multi-phase work, each step should include its intent, concrete validation criteria, and failure-detection signals, then be codified into a persistent reference document the system can use for future validation

System-supplied date values can drift across turns within a single session; documents created in later turns may receive different dates than earlier ones — re-read the current date rather than reusing one captured at session start

Building a UI that looks structurally correct (tabs, config sections, renders) but reads as a form viewer rather than an interactive tool means the user's intent — live customization with immediate feedback — was not modeled; implement the intent, not the structural shape
The agent must not declare code 'ready' or 'done' and allow it to be committed/pushed when it contains a known pattern violation that has already been corrected in prior sessions.
When the agent declares a test or feature 'successful', it must show actual output for the user to inspect rather than asserting success without evidence.

When the user explicitly invokes a mandatory skill like /atone, the agent must not skip or defer it — skipping a correction ritual while in the middle of being corrected is a compounding failure that erodes trust.

When a caching strategy invalidates a shared tag (e.g. `revalidateTag`), the agent must proactively surface the blast radius: one user's event invalidating cache state for all users is a critical design flaw that must be caught before implementation, not after.

When a report or doc introduces a named constant or config value (e.g. WORKER_MAX_DEFER_COUNT), it must define and explain what that value does inline; naming a config without explaining it forces the reader to hunt for meaning.

Before asking for permission to run a mutating command against an external service (render, vercel, cloud infra), show the exact command and a plain-English description of its effect; never prompt first and explain second.

Invoking /atone without completing the full event-recording flow (gathering context, picking a slug, running atone.sh add) leaves the mistake unrecorded and triggers a stop-hook gate on the next turn; the invocation and the recording must happen in the same turn.
Multi-agent task orchestration generates large volumes of task notification events; most are silently acknowledged without substantive processing
When user instructs 'commit and push', proceed directly without showing diffs or prompting for confirmation — user expects silent execution
User uses /core-dump proactively at session milestones and before exit, not just at end — treat it as a mid-session tool too
Sessions with many continuations (high 'this session being continued from' frequency) indicate context compaction happening often — proactive checkpointing reduces recovery overhead

When a circuit breaker or rate-limiting mechanism is scoped to a shared resource rather than a per-module or per-pipeline-step key, the agent must proactively flag that a failure in one consumer will block all other consumers — even those using different logic on the same dependency.

Silent zero-defaults in data extraction (e.g. `bb.get('x', 0)`) fabricate plausible-looking numeric values when source data is missing or partial, producing downstream motion/delta claims that are entirely fabricated rather than absent.

The agent should never commit or push for protected projects (those in an explicit protected-repos registry); it must prepare the change, show the diff, and hand the commit to the user. Authorization to commit elsewhere does not extend to protected repos.
When a user says a behavior is 'too noisy' or 'too aggressive', the correct response is to tune it down, not turn it off entirely — the complaint is a ceiling on intensity, not a removal mandate.
User reassurance ('I trust you', 'that's fine') is not authorization to remove safeguards, gates, or confirmations — it is social comfort, not a blanket removal mandate.

When a task list has not been updated across many turns but significant editing has occurred, the list has drifted from reality and must be reconciled before stopping — completed work marked done, new work added, in-progress set correctly.

When a feature unexpectedly requires adding a new library or dependency, the agent should surface this constraint to the user and offer a within-existing-dependency alternative first rather than proceeding with the addition.

One-off inline styling for a UI element (instead of reusing the existing component hover/interactive patterns) is a signal that there is a gap in the UI kit — surface this observation rather than writing one-off CSS.

Runtime dogfooding and live exercise catch bugs that a large test suite (99+ tests) misses; claimed correctness from test coverage alone is insufficient — actually running the affected path is a separate, necessary gate.

Config tools that perform validation only at parse time (not at write time) can silently break unrelated features when a required field is missing; always verify the full config profile loads correctly after editing, not just the targeted field.

A task list that accumulates many edits without corresponding TaskUpdate calls drifts into uselessness; the stop hook catching this after 20 edits and 8 turns confirms the failure mode is real and recurring.
In long parallel multi-agent sessions, writing a mini checkpoint after each discrete phase lets successor sessions restore context cheaply rather than rescanning the full codebase.
When building an access-gate system, unrecognized commands must default to DENY, not ALLOW; a default-allow fallback for unknown CLIs creates a bypass that renders the entire gate pointless.

Patching a specific instance of a policy violation (e.g., adding one CLI to a fallback list) without fixing the underlying class of problem (the structural default) leaves the same vulnerability open at every future unknown case.

Uncommitted agent edits to tracked files can be silently lost if the user commits or merges in a parallel operation; agent-made edits must be committed or explicitly stashed before handing control back to the user.

A Python exception class named 'NonRetryable' does not guarantee the framework skips retries; always read the error-handling code to confirm retry behavior rather than inferring it from the class name.
Vercel's auth.json stores `expiresAt` in seconds since epoch, not milliseconds; an off-by-1000x error in expiry calculations causes valid tokens to appear immediately expired.

When multiple agents work in parallel on the same codebase, they must pre-negotiate task ownership via IPC before starting work; overlapping claims without coordination produces muddy, conflicting edits that the user has to untangle.

The user prefers a breadth-first v1 pass across all surfaces before deep-diving into polish, validation, or improvements on individual items — pausing a sweep to perfect one area while others are unbuilt is the wrong priority order.

When sending IPC replies from a shell command, backticks and special characters in the message body get consumed by the shell and produce zero-byte or corrupted messages; the body must be quoted carefully or passed via a here-string or temp file.

When fixing a doc's voice by removing problematic content, do not overcorrect by stripping technical detail — target only the inappropriate content, not the technical framing; the fix should be scalpel-sized, not a full rewrite.
`rg -rn` is NOT 'recursive plus line-numbers' — the `-r` flag is `--replace`, which silently mangles output; always use `rg -n` for line numbers in recursive searches.

In a multi-agent setup where sessions are regularly context-cleared, each agent's checkpoint should record the peer agent's IPC alias so the next session can re-establish contact without requiring the user to re-introduce them.

A sub-agent must not touch or drop guard mute-files; a dropped mute file disables the guard machine-wide for all concurrent sessions until manually removed, silently negating safety gates the main agent relies on.

Code and docs can diverge between triage-time and edit-time; re-verify the specific file or function at the moment of writing the edit, not at the moment of planning it — the ground truth is the current file, not the earlier scan.

In a multi-agent parallel workflow, each agent's task list can become stale; before starting any item, verify it has not already been completed by a peer agent rather than relying on the list state from session start.

Advisory specs and skill docs only bind agents that read them at startup; to make a behavioral constraint effective across sub-agents and in-flight sessions, enforcement must be placed at the data-write layer (a hook, CLI gate, or schema check) rather than left as advisory text.

When writing a document that will be shared externally, all internal banter, critique, and conversational framing about stakeholders must be stripped before the document is written — the agent must distinguish between what was said conversationally and what is safe to publish.

Correcting a document's tone for its audience should adjust register only, not strip technical substance — overcorrecting toward accessible prose leaves engineers with an essay they will abandon for lacking implementation detail.

When asking the user a decision question, include enough background and tradeoffs to make the question self-contained and answerable without additional follow-up; questions that force the user to ask for context before answering are a recurring friction point.

In multi-agent IPC sessions, unanswered peer queries must be replied to before the session ends; stop hooks will fire repeatedly for each unreplied message, indicating this is a mechanical obligation, not optional.

Task list hygiene degrades specifically during high-parallelism periods with many sub-agent completions; the task list must be explicitly reconciled after a burst of sub-agent work, not only at session boundaries.

When verifying IPC message delivery, wait for an actual round-trip reply from the peer rather than inspecting the sending agent's own logs or send-side telemetry — a successful send does not prove the message arrived or was acted on.

In multi-agent sessions, the user should not have to repeatedly give plain go-aheads for short-distance progress; batch sequential work into autonomous runs and halt only at genuine decision points, blocking reviews, or missing user input.

CLI authentication commands (e.g. cloud provider logins) require an interactive terminal and cannot be automated; flag this to the user up front and hand off the auth step rather than attempting it and failing.

In multi-agent IPC setups where sessions are cleared periodically, registered aliases become stale after the owning session restarts; fall back to bare sessionId addressing for reliable delivery rather than trusting previously-registered aliases.

The Task tool must be updated incrementally throughout active work, not only at major milestones; allowing many edits to accumulate without reflecting them in the task list causes the live status view to drift and confuses both the user and future turns.

When proposing names for packages, repos, or identifiers within the same organization, always default to a consistent naming scheme across sibling artifacts — suggesting diverging names in the same namespace without an explicit justification draws immediate pushback.

While waiting for a peer agent to send information over an IPC channel, the agent should not repeatedly nudge the user for context or status updates — ask once, then wait for the real message rather than turning the user into a polling proxy.

Git branch state captured at session start can silently drift during the session; always re-read current branch state immediately before any branch-sensitive operation rather than relying on the value observed at session open.

When sending IPC messages between peer agents, the agent must verify the peer alias maps to the intended recipient by checking live peer IDs before sending — a descriptive alias name does not guarantee it identifies the correct session.

During autonomous multi-turn work sessions, the task list must be updated after each logical unit of work rather than batching updates at session end — allowing the task list to drift from actual progress renders the live status surface useless.

Shared UI elements such as navigation shells must be implemented from a single shared source component, not replicated per-page, so that all authenticated pages remain consistent without manual propagation.

When a component returns no data, downstream derivation logic must emit an empty or uncertain result rather than converting the absence into a fabricated negative claim; treating an empty result as evidence of non-existence produces false negatives that are indistinguishable from real negative evidence.

When a test lab or pipeline has long-lived caches, re-running it after a code change exercises the cache layer rather than the changed code; confirming a code change requires a cache-bust parameter or explicit cache invalidation before treating re-run results as evidence the fix works.

When the user reports a UI component inconsistency on one page (sidebar, drawer, modal shell), the fix must be applied to all pages using that component simultaneously; treating it as a single-page fix while sibling pages still use incompatible variants is a failure the user experiences as a missed-obvious pattern.

When a list page lacks pagination and other list pages in the same codebase already implement it, the agent must apply the pagination pattern without being explicitly told; the sibling-page pattern is available in-session evidence that must be used.

When a UI standardization request arrives as a list of issues across multiple pages, the agent should sweep ALL pages that use the affected component, not only the pages named in the user's message — the named examples are a sample, not an exhaustive scope.

When the agent pauses mid-task without surfacing a reason, the user must ask why, consuming a check-in round-trip; agents should explicitly state the stopping condition (blocker, phase boundary, question needed) before halting execution.

CSS utility class names used in implementations should be confirmed as present in the project's actual stylesheet or framework configuration before use; names that look like valid defaults may not be available in a project using a custom subset.

When an agent edits source files and then claims success using words like 'done', 'works', 'fixed', or 'passing' without actually executing the changed code path, it constitutes a false completion claim — type-checking, linting, and collecting tests are not substitutes for running the code.

Under high edit velocity (many file changes per turn), the agent's task list drifts from actual work done — the discipline that holds at low throughput is the first to slip when editing pace accelerates, requiring external hooks to force reconciliation.

When a list page is missing pagination and sibling list pages in the same codebase already display the paginated pattern, the agent must apply the same pagination before returning — treating each page in isolation when the pattern is already proven nearby is a systematic miss.

PR comments and inline docstrings should be stripped to the minimum non-obvious WHY; essay-length comments on small or self-evident changes are treated as noise and removed, not appreciated as thoroughness.
When presenting deferred decision items to the user, the agent omits the prior decision context and concrete options, forcing the user to ask a follow-up question before they can act.

When a main orchestrator session hits its usage limit while sub-agents are waiting on IPC responses, sub-agents are left blocked indefinitely; the architecture must anticipate this by having sub-agents self-report idle state so they can be re-queued on resume.

After a correction that a UI component must be globally shared, the agent must search and fix ALL instances across the entire codebase in the same response — patching only the immediate callsite while leaving sibling pages broken is experienced as gaslighting, not progress.

UI review reports generated by testing in only one visual mode (e.g., dark mode only) produce findings the user considers not useful; review findings must be annotated with which mode was observed, or the review must cover both modes before reporting.

When a sub-agent hits a credential or auth block that is outside its own scope to fix, the correct behavior is to surface the exact command the user needs to run and hold explicitly — not attempt workarounds or stall silently.

When a sub-agent's write is hard-blocked by a harness guard, the correct recovery is to return the full findings as text in the response so the parent session can persist them — the harness block is not a failure, it is an enforced handoff point.
When the user asks for a tracking artifact for their own reference, provide a human-facing doc they can independently consult, explicitly separate from agent-internal memory or task state.

When a user asks to set up 'runtime variables' or 'runtime config' in an already-deployed app, they typically mean dynamically-adjustable application-level globals (feature flags, model keys, prompts, thresholds) — not deployment-time environment variables or secret managers. Proposing env-var or external secret solutions to this request is a category error.

When the user sets an explicit narrow scope for a feature ('only for X, not Y'), the implementation must enforce that scope literally without adding self-gating flexibility or generalizing beyond what was stated.

Before proposing to re-enable or expand a disabled configuration (CI trigger, feature flag, auto-run), investigate why it was disabled — the existing disabled state may represent a deliberate architectural or cost decision.
When a sub-agent signals completion via notification, verify the output artifact exists on disk before using its findings — the notification is not proof the file was written.

When a PR review or code audit output is delivered as a pipe-delimited dump or HTML artifact, the user prefers inline markdown organized by logical/functional category, with severity only explicitly marked for high-severity findings rather than used as the primary sorting axis.

The user prefers a deferred 'to be reviewed' staging area for completed non-critical work rather than requesting immediate review for every change; items get crossed off once actually inspected, not when the agent marks them done.
The user expects commit messages to exclude model co-authorship metadata (Co-Authored-By lines, session URL footers) and wants a comment hygiene pass applied at commit time.

When an agent creates a formal or technical document to capture and systematize an existing system (e.g., a concepts/schema doc derived from the codebase), that derivative document must never be used as the authoritative specification in gap audits or feature planning — the original user-authored product spec remains the upstream authority, and citing agent-authored formalizations as the source inverts the derivation chain.

When a sub-agent performing a gap or capability audit independently selects an agent-authored formalization document as its authority (rather than the user-authored product spec), the parent agent must validate what ground-truth document the sub-agent used before consuming or acting on the audit findings — acting on a report grounded in a derived, agent-authored doc inverts the authority chain.

When the agent ships UI features (labels, flows, module names) without consulting design mocks, the result mismatches user expectations; the agent must read the design mocks before implementing any named UI element.

IPC message delivery should be confirmed by waiting for an actual round-trip reply from the peer, not by inspecting the sending agent's own logs; the user will reject log-based assurance and insist on a verified reply.

When a list page is missing pagination and sibling list pages in the same session already display the paginated pattern, the agent should recognise and apply that pattern rather than treating each page in isolation; in-session context that directly proves the pattern is available evidence the agent must use.

When a sub-agent hits a credential or auth block that is outside its own scope to fix, it should surface the exact command the user needs to run and hold explicitly — not attempt workarounds or silently stall.

Deferred decision items presented to the user must include the exact prior decision or constraint and at least two concrete options to choose from — items without that context force a follow-up round-trip and are experienced as an incomplete handoff.

When a multi-agent orchestration session hits its usage limit mid-coordination, sub-agents left waiting have no path to notify the orchestrator; the architecture should include idle-notification so the orchestrator can re-queue them on resume rather than leaving them hanging.

Declaring implementation work done without verifying on the actual running dev server leads to issues (wrong labels still showing, removed pages still present) that only surface when the user manually checks.

Product-level behavioral decisions embedded in implementation (e.g., whether a user can add files to an existing job) must be surfaced as explicit questions to the user rather than resolved silently as implementation choices.

When conducting a gap audit against product requirements, the agent must use the user-authored upstream source document as authoritative, not a downstream technical-definitions doc the agent itself generated from that source.
UI module labels, naming, and creation flows must be validated against the design mocks before shipping, not derived from internal naming conventions or prior code patterns alone.

When the user explicitly grants permission to proceed autonomously on reversible work due to time pressure or personal constraints, the agent should proceed without seeking further clarification — waiting is the wrong move.

When presenting deferred decision items to the user, each item must include the exact prior decision or constraint and at least two concrete options; items without that context force an unnecessary follow-up round-trip and are experienced as an incomplete handoff.

When a sub-agent hits a credential or auth block that is outside its own scope to fix, it should surface the exact command the user needs to run and hold — not attempt workarounds — so the human can unblock it in one action.

When a list page is missing pagination and sibling list pages in the same application already display a paginated pattern, the agent must apply the same pattern before returning rather than treating each page in isolation.
Completion and gap assessments made without reading actual source files consistently overestimate how much is built; the agent should read code before producing a gap table.
The user prefers a deferred review workflow: completed non-critical items should be queued to a 'to be reviewed' backlog rather than triggering an immediate review unless explicitly asked.

Implementing UI module labels, page names, and creation flows without first consulting the design mocks causes explicit user frustration and complete rework; the mocks must be consulted before any UI label or flow is shipped, not derived from internal naming conventions.

When an agent has authored a downstream formalization document from a user-authored product spec, feature gap audits must be grounded in the original user-authored document; using the agent-generated derivative as the authoritative reference produces incorrect completeness verdicts.

When a skill invocation has a documented mandatory gate phase (e.g., adversarial validation), silently skipping it and marking tasks complete on the board is a confirmed mistake — the gate exists precisely because the agent would otherwise declare success prematurely.

When a project-specific UI verification checklist is available, the agent must run it during any browser verification pass — skipping a context-specific checklist while doing browser verification on the same page is treated as a serious failure, not a minor omission.

Claiming a specific UI sub-issue is fixed without verifying the full rendered state of the containing element leads to adjacent problems surviving — the agent fixed one thing (copy) while breaking another (title) and leaving a third (padding) untouched, then reported success.

User-facing UI banner copy written in formal, structured agent-style language ('This job has not started — it needs its setup.') reads as AI-generated and is rejected; the user expects short, natural human phrasing even for system-state messages.

When the user types a terse continuation signal ('proceed', 'keep going') and context pressure is below 70%, the agent must continue work immediately without pausing to ask clarifying questions — pausing on a terse continuation at low context is a confirmed mistake, not a safe default.
When a list page is missing standard pagination while sibling list pages already implement it, the agent leaves the gap uncorrected and waits for the user to point it out explicitly.

A sub-agent that hits a credential or auth block outside its own scope should surface the exact unblocking command the user needs to run and hold — not attempt workarounds — enabling the user to unblock the flow in one action and the sub-agent to resume cleanly.

When incorporating a dead or unavailable peer agent's work, selectively triage it for only the parts worth integrating rather than wholesale adopting it; the user's framing 'only where worth it' signals selective, not additive, integration

Null or missing fields in a data pipeline must be explicitly handled before numeric operations or display logic — when the agent notices a null coercion producing a suspicious default value during a pre-delivery review, it must treat that as a blocker, not dismiss it as acceptable, even if it was previously corrected elsewhere in the pipeline.

When implementing a multi-criteria filter (e.g. job type exclusions), the agent must verify that ALL stated criteria are enforced conjunctively against real output before delivery — a filter that passes obviously out-of-scope items was never exercised against the actual dataset.

When the agent claims to have read through produced output before delivery, that claim must be backed by actually reading the rows and acting on what is found — stating 'I noticed X but dismissed it as acceptable' after an explicit prior correction on X is the same failure mode as not reading at all.

In high-activity sessions with many sequential file edits, the task list must be reconciled before stopping rather than allowed to drift — a task list frozen across 50+ edits leaves the user's TUI blind and signals the agent has lost track of its own progress.

UI elements with content that is statically known at render time (sidebar navigation, topbar branding, page titles) must never receive skeleton loading states — skeletons are reserved for data that is asynchronously fetched.

When multiple pages each need a loading skeleton, each page must implement its own page-specific skeleton that mirrors that page's actual content structure; reusing a different page's skeleton component on the wrong route is a critical visual defect.

Using an IIFE or scope-wrapper in JSX is a recurring smell; before inserting one, scan the 10 lines around the insertion point and conform to whatever pattern siblings use (inline prop or plain const).

When the user states requirements in an explicit order, skipping or deprioritizing the first requirement while completing later items is treated as a significant failure; user-stated ordering is a hard priority constraint, not a loose suggestion.

Hitting a model subscription or usage limit mid-autonomous-session causes the session to stall silently rather than producing a graceful notification and fallback, leaving pending work in an indeterminate state.

When presenting deferred decision items to the user, each item must include the exact prior decision context that triggered the deferral and at least two concrete options — items without that context force an unnecessary follow-up round-trip.

The user prefers completed non-critical items to be added to a deferred 'to be reviewed' backlog rather than surfaced for immediate review. Items in the backlog are crossed off when the user personally verifies them, not when the agent completes them.

Autonomous deploy steps that require interactive browser-based authentication (OAuth flows) block the agent session and cannot be made truly async without pre-establishing credentials or using a service-account-based alternative.

Validating another agent's output against standing project constraints (e.g. style rules, UI invariants) before merging or shipping catches violations that the producing agent's own checks would miss.

Infrastructure documentation such as deploy strategies and pipeline configurations should be written in project-visible locations, not only inside agent-internal directories, so the team can reference them independently of the agent.

Interactive authentication flows embedded in deployment scripts (browser-redirect OAuth, gcloud auth login) block autonomous agent sessions from completing deploy tasks; the user explicitly wants fully async deploy pipelines that do not require human credential intervention mid-session.

When a scraping or data pipeline produces zero results for a specific source, the agent should proactively surface which pages or endpoints were checked, not just the zero count — the user will ask for this detail as a separate follow-up otherwise.

When a filtering UI is built over data aggregated from multiple heterogeneous sources, omitting a per-source filter for any actively-scraped source is immediately noticed and criticized by the user, even when other filters exist

Dispatching a sub-agent with 'exclusive use' of a browser MCP resource without first verifying no other session or agent currently holds it causes the new agent to block for its entire wait period with no autonomous recovery path

Even when a global default (e.g. public repository visibility) is configured, the agent should ask about or confirm the preference when creating a specific new repository, because the user's intent for that repo may differ from the global default.

IIFE and scope-wrapper expressions inside JSX are a recurring code smell in this codebase; when sibling elements use inline props or plain const declarations, the agent should conform to that existing pattern rather than introducing a wrapper function.

When a dead sibling agent's plan is handed to a new session for triage, the receiving agent should evaluate each item independently against the current plan rather than wholesale importing it — the user expects selective incorporation of only what is worth merging.
Marking a task as done in the task list without having actually verified its completion is a false report that the user treats as a reporting error requiring explicit correction and /atone.
Idle notifications arriving from sub-agents that have already been TaskStopped are stale and should be immediately dismissed without action or reassignment; a stopped seat's ping carries no new work.

Multiple decisions required from the user should be collected through a decision wizard (inline menu or pre-answered form), never as a numbered list of questions in chat — the user has explicitly requested this be a durable rule.

When a task list goes many turns without updates while edits accumulate, it drifts into misleading state; the agent must reconcile completed and newly-added work into the task tool frequently, not at the end of a long run.

Choosing an HTML artifact format over markdown when markdown would have sufficed is a format overshoot; when HTML is chosen for any output, the mandatory light/dark toggle must be present or the artifact is treated as incomplete.
Do not pause to ask for clarification on terse continuation signals ('proceed', 'keep going', 'yes') when context is well below pressure thresholds and there is clearly pending work on the task list

Domain-specific filtering pipelines must be spot-checked against real output data before delivery — if obviously out-of-scope items appear in the results, the filter logic was never exercised against the actual dataset.

When model subscription limits or organization access restrictions are hit during autonomous long-running sessions, the agent should notify the user explicitly and stop gracefully rather than silently failing or retrying on the same blocked model.

When a data-source filtering UI is built over data aggregated from multiple heterogeneous platforms, omitting a per-source filter for any actively-scraped source is immediately noticed and criticized by the user — even if other filters exist.

When assessing context capacity, the agent must rely exclusively on the ctx-pressure hook's fired notifications (at 70/80/90%) as the only valid instrument — not tool count, turn count, or a felt sense of fullness. Raising a context warning when the hook has not fired is a false flag and a known recurring mistake.

When the agent already holds the full result set in its tool output, substituting a curated subset or summary in the reply is a substitution error — the user asked for the data, not the agent's editorial of it.

The task list must be updated continuously during active editing work, not only at turn boundaries; when many edits happen without task updates, the list drifts and loses its value as a live status surface.

When the agent explains a technical error or diagnosis, delivering the explanation in compressed or indirect language (rather than stating plainly what broke and why) causes the user to file corrections and explicitly demand plain speech; the reply's structure should lead with the root cause in one sentence, not defer it behind qualifications or jargon.

When a sub-agent sends a repeat idle notification after already delivering its result and being stopped, the correct response is to note it as a stale signal and take no action rather than re-querying or re-dispatching.

When a sub-agent sends an idle notification, the agent should verify that the expected output file actually exists on disk before treating the work as done; the idle signal alone does not prove the output was written.

When the declared-ready hook fires after a turn that only edited documentation or markdown files (no source or test files), the agent should surface the false positive plainly rather than treating it as a real code-verification requirement.

When asserting that a file, route, or code path does not exist, the agent must run an ignore-transparent search (e.g., rg --no-ignore) before making the claim — default search tools silently skip gitignored and hidden files, causing false absence claims.

When a multi-seat research fan-out completes, the synthesizing agent must re-confirm the target project scope before writing the final report — not just at dispatch time — because findings from sibling projects can contaminate the synthesis if the scope check is omitted at the write step.

The user prefers maintaining a 'to be reviewed' backlog for completed non-critical work rather than pausing for immediate review; completed items go to that queue unless the user explicitly asks for immediate review.
Running an explicit pre-deploy constraint check against a sub-agent's output (rather than trusting the sub-agent's self-report of correctness) catches style and invariant violations before they ship.

When the user explicitly grants broad authorization multiple times (e.g., 'Proceed with all'), the agent must not invent new blocking gates for sub-items — repeated explicit authorization is a standing go, not an invitation to find new reasons to pause.

The user prefers the agent to complete all obvious sequential steps autonomously without checkpoint confirmations between them; asking for approval on each individually wastes turns and the user has stated this directly.

After verifying a sub-agent's output file exists on disk, immediately TaskStop the seat in the same turn. An idle seat with a verified output can be commandeered by a board auto-dispatcher; closing it is the correct completion step, not an optional cleanup.

When presenting deferred decision items to the user, each item must include the exact prior decision or constraint plus concrete selectable options; items without that context force a follow-up round-trip before the user can act.
During long autonomous sessions with many tool calls, the agent's task list drifts from what it is actually doing, requiring external hook intervention to force reconciliation.

When a data-source filtering UI is built over data aggregated from multiple heterogeneous platforms, omitting a per-source filter for any actively-scraped source is immediately noticed and criticized by the user, even when other cross-source filters exist.

When asked to document plans or contracts, the output must be architecture diagrams, API payload shape tables, and JSON examples — not a summary of current project deployment status; conflating the two forces a correction round-trip.

When the user responds to an agent pause with 'keep going' or invokes /atone for stubbornness, the prior stop was unjustified; re-raising the same soft blocker after an explicit 'keep going' is a repeated failure warranting an S3 atone entry.

When claiming a module, file, or directory does not exist, the agent must run an ignore-transparent search (rg/fd --no-ignore or equivalent) before asserting absence; a default search silently skips gitignored and hidden paths, producing a confident false negative.

When idle notifications arrive from sub-agents that have already been explicitly stopped, the correct response is to dismiss them as stale without re-dispatching or reacting — acting on a stale idle signal wastes a seat and can reopen completed work.

Treating a --dry-run as verification of real deployment is a false confidence claim: dry-run only prints commands without executing them, so declaring a deploy 'confirmed' based on dry-run output is wrong even when the output looks correct.

Before justifying a design choice with cost reasoning (e.g., 'we use a simpler path to keep costs down'), the agent must verify which option is actually cheaper — asserting cost motivation without checking relative pricing is a structural claim without reading the evidence.

When verifying a UI surface, the agent must read the specific element the complaint targets (e.g., rows) rather than a nearby but different element (e.g., a panel or header), or the check passes while the defect remains visible.

When synthesizing multi-agent research output, the agent must verify which project/domain the synthesis is for before writing, not infer it from the agents' findings alone; a mismatched synthesis produces work the user must entirely discard.

Idle sub-agents that have completed their scoped work must be stopped immediately after their output is verified; a seat left running can be commandeered by board auto-dispatchers and do unassigned work.

When the user explicitly rules an item closed and says never to raise it again, the agent must record that ruling durably; re-raising it in a future turn signals the ruling was never stored, which the user treats as both a record-keeping failure and a time-wasting offense.

When status replies lead with narrating what the agent did rather than stating the two or three facts the user needs to act on, the user consistently rejects the response even when the underlying work is correct.

When the agent explicitly cites a prior mistake pattern in its own output and then produces the same shape in the same turn, this is the most severe form of pattern recurrence — the correction was processed but not internalized, and the juror rates it very-wrong at high confidence.

Default LLM prose register — excessive bold spans, Label:fragment rows instead of full sentences, not-X-but-Y contrast scaffolds — is consistently flagged by stop hooks and corrected; plain prose with meaning first and no decoration is required.

When presenting a list of deferred decision items to the user, each item must include the exact prior decision or constraint and concrete options; items without that context force a follow-up round-trip before the user can answer and are experienced as an incomplete handoff.

A function return type annotation that silently diverges from the actual return arity (e.g., annotated as 2-tuple but returning 3-tuple) is invisible without a configured static type checker and will crash callers at runtime; projects without mypy or pyright have no backstop and are especially vulnerable to this class of bug.

When implementing a UI shell component (sidebar, drawer, modal) on one page, the agent must audit all sibling pages for the same component before writing any code — implementing per-page variants of a globally-shared shell is a systematic error, not an isolated miss.

Gap analysis and completion assessments that have not been grounded in actual code reads tend to overestimate how much is built. The agent should default to checking the running app or source before claiming an item is complete in a status report.

Goal statements written as passive perfect-tense declarations ('X has been completed', 'Y is done') fail to satisfy the user; they must be active behavioral statements describing what the agent will proactively do going forward.

Goal statements written as flowing behavioral prose become uncheckable; the user prefers short, concrete declarative sentences where any reader can look at one named thing and say yes or no at the moment of reading.

When design mocks are referenced as the design authority throughout a codebase, the agent must read them before implementing any UI element names, labels, or structures — skipping this step produces naming that diverges from the agreed design and requires manual correction by the user.
UI module labels, naming, and job-creation flows must be validated against design mocks before shipping, not derived from internal naming conventions or prior code patterns.

Claiming UI fixes are done without exercising the actual rendered page leads to multiple issues surviving — UI work is only verified when the page is visually inspected in a running browser, not when the code change looks correct

Before declaring a UI change complete, the agent must manually exercise every interactive surface touched — including modals, dropdowns, and navigation flows — not just the primary visible state; unexercised modals represent silent defects.

When a stop hook fires for a prose violation and the agent rewrites the reply, it frequently regenerates the same violations rather than actually fixing them — the rewrite is cosmetic, not corrective.

The 'Generated with Claude Code' harness trailer appears in PR descriptions even when it is explicitly banned in project configuration, indicating the agent defaults to harness behavior over project-specific overrides.

The declared-ready hook continues to fire multiple times within a single session even after earlier block events, indicating the pattern of claiming success without exercising the code path is not self-correcting within a turn and requires repeated external enforcement.

Even when prose-style rules are enforced by hooks, the agent regresses to default-LLM register (em-dashes, label:fragment rows, bolded bullet armies) in multi-turn sessions where the output accumulates incrementally rather than being drafted at once.

When the user asks to see specific data or results, the agent must present that data directly rather than describing it cryptically or summarizing it at one level of abstraction removed from what was requested.
Having a file name or symbol appear in grep/search output does not constitute reading that file; the agent should read the actual file before making claims about the behavior it implements.

When a software dependency (model weights, binaries, large assets) must be downloaded at runtime and that download can time out or cause chaos, the correct design response is a pre-flight check that fails fast rather than allowing the feature to run in a broken half-downloaded state.

For collaborative repos where multiple contributors work in parallel, establishing a named base branch at major feature checkpoints improves merge conflict isolation and lets parallel tracks merge independently rather than racing on the same target.

When the user asks a delegation or scoping question (e.g., 'what do you truly need me for?'), the correct response is a brief enumeration of owner-only actions, not operational runbooks or instructions that contain non-owner steps.

A goal statement or status claim that is directly contradicted by data the agent itself rendered in the same turn (e.g., a table of open work) is a self-refuting claim and should be caught before sending.
The user explicitly rejects HTML artifacts for code review reports in favor of inline markdown rendered directly in the conversation.

When the agent spends significant tokens on UI changes but produces no visible improvement (or fixes only its own same-session regressions), the user treats it as a waste; UI work requires visual verification against actual user-visible outcomes before claiming done.

Iterating on UI changes without a mechanism to visually verify the result wastes tokens and fails to make real progress; the agent should acknowledge when it cannot verify UI changes rather than continuing to apply blind edits.

A fresh adversarial reviewer sub-agent reliably catches HIGH-severity bugs in code the main agent just wrote; dispatching one immediately after implementing a complex feature is a high-ROI verification step.

Holding independent judgment and debating a proposed design decision rather than capitulating is explicitly valued; the user expects the agent to push back with evidence even after a reviewer or prior session recommended otherwise.

Retrieval confidence is more trustworthy when computed from retrieval metrics (cosine score plus margin to the second result) than from the model's self-reported confidence, which tends to be overconfident.

When multiple agents need concurrent browser access, running duplicate dev servers on different ports gives each agent its own session without contention; the port-assignment overhead is lower than the coordination overhead of time-sharing one server.

Reporting a system capability as 'live' or 'working' without runtime verification (e.g., when required env vars were visibly absent from the runner environment) is a structural claim without evidence — the check must actually be executed, not inferred from code presence.

When an explicit length or format directive is given ('if nothing has changed, say so in one line'), that directive overrides the agent's instinct to produce a full-structured response — violating it even with real content is a protocol failure, not thoroughness.

When the owner-gated or blocking item exists in a report, it must lead the reply — self-correction paragraphs and context preamble placed before the actionable item are a dense-briefing failure regardless of how thorough the analysis is.
When a task is complete, the agent should report the result and stop; offering a menu of next-step forks at the end of a completed task is an anti-pattern the user explicitly rejects.
File Tools MCP `list_sheets`/`read_tabular` can fail on .xlsx files with a runtime error; keep a pandas fallback for spreadsheet reading tasks when the MCP path is unreliable.

The user prefers a 'to be reviewed later' queue for completed non-critical work rather than requesting immediate review of each deliverable; items park there until the user explicitly checks them off.

Before referencing a specific numbered artifact (PR, issue, ticket) in a repo the agent is already making API calls to, the agent must verify that artifact actually exists in that repo — asserting a PR number without checking is a verifiable error that one extra call would have caught.

A decision page answer of 'Neither' or any rejection of all presented options is NOT an approval to ship any of them; the agent must read the selected answer literally and treat a non-selection as a block, not as permission to pick the closest option.
Asserting a resource is unused without reading the file that references it is a structural claim without code evidence — the specific file must be read before the claim can be made.
Running the same script as both the action and the verification probe is not independent verification: two invocations of one instrument cannot detect a bug in that instrument itself.

A PR declared green based only on a local test run is not verified if CI is running a different test suite; the agent must check CI job results, not just local execution, before claiming a PR is ready.

Before directing the owner to use a UI surface for decisions, the agent must exercise that surface (e.g., curl or screenshot) to confirm it is functional, not merely that the code that generates it was written.

The user prefers a breadth-first v1 pass across all surfaces before deep-diving into polish, validation, or improvement on individual items; pausing a sweep to perfect one area while others are unbuilt is the wrong priority order.

When sending IPC replies from a shell command, backticks and special characters in the message body get consumed by the shell and produce zero-byte or corrupted messages; quote the body carefully or use a here-string.

The user prefers the agent to explore and ground itself in the existing codebase and surface a recommendation before touching code; jumping directly to edits without that grounding phase is a recurring correction.

The autocorrect hinter can corrupt bash command output text (e.g., mangling tool names into unrelated strings), making shell-captured output unreliable; use the Read tool to read file contents rather than trusting bash text.

Session-scoped stop hooks with explicit, verifiable completion conditions (e.g., 'must pass /ui-gripe before marking done') effectively prevent premature task closure in long autonomous sessions where the agent might self-declare success.

During extended autonomous work with a stop-hook condition, the task list drifts from actual work done; the agent should update task status proactively after each logical unit of work rather than batching updates at session end.

A primary orchestrating agent that spends its turns only relaying IPC messages between peer agents without doing its own substantive work will be explicitly called out; the orchestrating agent must maintain and advance its own work items even while coordinating peers.

Halting mid-task without a specific, genuine blocker that only the user can resolve wastes the user's attention budget; the threshold for pausing must be high — only when the agent literally cannot proceed without a human decision.

Authorship or attribution claims (who wrote a file, which agent created an artifact) require verifiable evidence such as git blame or file:line citation; mtime alone is insufficient and stating it as fact to the owner is a mistake.

Printing a goal-proposal paste line and ending the turn without making any tool call is treated as a stop by the harness; the agent must begin working toward the proposed goal in the same turn rather than waiting for the owner to arm it.

Applying a hard line cap to a checkpoint or context summary silently drops load-bearing constraints that fall outside the cap; constraints must be preserved verbatim regardless of summary length limits, and line caps should never be the mechanism that decides what stays.

Peer agent IPC queries received during a turn must be explicitly answered before the turn ends; an unanswered query is a broken contract with the peer agent, and a stop hook reminder counts as only one warning — the reply must go out before stopping.

Declaring a fix 'safe' or 'resolved' across multiple sessions without mechanical verification allows the same failure to recur; when the user reports the same problem after multiple claimed fixes, the agent must treat this as a verification failure, not an explanation opportunity.

Listing a SKILL.md's sub-skill names as evidence that a skill was invoked and resolved is not equivalent to actually running the skill and observing its output; the agent's own documentation is not proof of execution.
When prior research artifacts exist in the session, the agent must read and incorporate them before dispatching new sub-agents for overlapping questions, rather than re-deriving the same findings.

The agent repeatedly claimed work was complete without actually executing the changed code path, triggering the declared-ready gate more than once in the same session; each firing is a new failure, not the same one caught twice.

When the user has already granted explicit permission in-session and the agent continues to hesitate, add steps, or ask follow-up questions before acting, it violates the authority-already-held principle; the user experiences it as the agent making a simple task unnecessarily hard.

A status reply whose first line narrates what the agent did rather than what is live, what works, and what the user must act on forces a re-ask and is a recurring failure even when all the correct information eventually appears lower in the reply.

Knowing a relevant fact on record (from a prior tool result, earlier message, or context) without running the single verification check that would confirm or disprove it is treated as a real mistake even when the general diagnosis is correct.

Bash command chaining with &&, ;, or pipes persists even when the agent has just written or acknowledged the rule banning it; the rule binding as text without a mechanical stop is insufficient to prevent the behavior.

When the agent prints a /goal paste line and ends the turn without making further tool calls, it violates the 'propose, do not arm' rule — a goal proposal is not a stop point; the agent must continue working toward it immediately.

When multiple agents run in parallel on the same codebase, they must pre-negotiate task ownership via IPC before starting work; overlapping claims without coordination produces muddy, conflicting edits that the user has to untangle.

A full-file rewrite makes the agent the author of all preserved content, including existing voice, conventions, and style — the entire file must be reviewed after the rewrite, not just the changed sections.

When dispatching gemini sub-agents for large-scale transcript or corpus analysis, running a small test dispatch first before committing to the full fleet reduces wasted cost on prompt or tool errors that only surface at scale.

During autonomous multi-turn sessions with many sequential edits, the Task tool list drifts from actual work in progress; the agent should update task statuses within every 2-3 substantive edits, not batch updates at the end of a work block.
UI changes signed off as verified after testing only the dark theme reliably produce broken light-theme regressions that are caught in review; both themes must be exercised before claiming done.

When a user asks what was done and what is next, narrating the agent's intermediate steps, tool-call history, or context spend instead of stating current state and next action is a dense-briefing failure.

When asked a concise factual question, the agent responds with a lengthy essay including unrelated context (proposal IDs, RCA paths, peer message digests) that the user did not request, burying or omitting the direct answer entirely.

Interactive input MCP tools and structured-choice prompts cannot be used when the user is in TUI fullscreen mode; the user cannot select options and must reject and answer in prose, so any structured input in that context will silently fail.

Small fast models (e.g. gemini-3.5-flash) can match or outperform flagship models on closed-set classification tasks while costing significantly less; default model selection should not assume that harder tasks always require larger models.

Establishing a shared nomenclature or vocabulary document as a deliverable alongside an implementation plan helps validate cross-agent consistency and gives both agents and reviewers a stable reference for terminology during execution.

Dispatching gemini sub-agents to scan historical session transcripts is an effective recovery pattern when the current session has lost context about prior task state or accumulated feedback across many past sessions.

Running an adversarial review pass against the agent's own synthesis documents (design proposals, plans, specs) catches motivated reasoning that self-review within the same context misses — independent skeptic framing on your own output is a reliable quality gate.

When prompting the gemini lane, avoid `@`-prefixed package names or scoped identifiers directly in the prompt body — the CLI parses them as image-attach tokens and silently corrupts the intended text.

When the user names specific deployment environments in a comparison or verification request, the agent must confirm which environment each data arm actually came from before reporting done; substituting a local or engine-flipped run for a named deployed environment is a literal-request-over-intent failure.

Adding a scheduled warm-up or pre-load job for a tool (e.g. ollama warm-morning) without explicit user request is unprompted infra scope creep; the user expects models and services to load on first use, never on boot unless explicitly configured

Removing or overwriting a code comment or annotation that explicitly encoded a hard constraint (e.g. 'no-shift', 'reserved') without asking is treated as a serious violation even when the surrounding code change is otherwise correct.
Advertising a localhost URL in a reply without first navigating to it and exercising its primary action is a recurring failure mode; the user's first click tends to fail when this shortcut is taken.
The user explicitly rejects hedged or softened blocker language — genuine blockers must be called out directly as blockers, not softened into observations or qualifications.

When the owner's stated priority is a primary deliverable, pivoting to fix a minor peripheral issue (a test, a lint error, a small debt item) and spending multiple turns on it counts as scope deviation and earns an explicit correction.

Printing a /goal paste line and ending the turn counts as a stop attempt, not work — the agent must make the next tool call toward the proposed goal in the same turn, or say one line explaining the genuine blocker.

The agent defaults to default-LLM register prose (em-dashes, excess bold spans, decorative markers like ★) even when a style ledger bans them; this requires a Stop hook to catch, suggesting the generation-time filter is not reliable without mechanical enforcement.

In multi-agent sessions where context is regularly cleared, core-dump and checkpoint artifacts should explicitly capture peer agent IPC aliases and session IDs so successor sessions can re-establish connections without user intervention.

Keying each result in a batch job by (judge + item + discriminating labels) enables resuming mid-run on abort or API error without re-paying already-completed work — build resumable caches for expensive fan-out jobs.

When a hook has a high fire-rate but zero conversions, verify the hook is attached to the correct event type before attributing the failure to implementation — an event type mismatch means the hook fires on unintended triggers while the intended events are never caught.

For fan-out scraping pipelines the user prefers routing the raw collection step to a lower-tier model (sonnet-high or gemini) while reserving higher-tier models for analysis and judgment stages as an explicit cost optimization

When a fable-tier agent delegates its primary authoring work to a lower-tier sub-agent instead of doing it itself, the agent violates the model-tier routing intent; fable seats are dispatched for involved work they perform themselves, not to orchestrate lower tiers for the same work.

The user prefers the agent to batch sequential work and only halt at genuine decision points or critical reviews, not at every short distance for lightweight go-aheads that force the user to context-switch repeatedly.

When the agent generates ranked or enumerated output, it must read through the produced list before delivery — claiming an output is ready without having personally read the rows is the same failure mode as claiming code works without running it.

The user treats visual consistency from the customer's perspective as an absolute requirement that overrides implementation differences between surfaces or tech stacks; framing an inconsistency as a tech-stack difference is not an acceptable justification.

The agent's self-critical response to a major correction often describes rigor without demonstrating it: it names what it should have checked but does not run those checks before sending, which the user experiences as covering tracks rather than honest RCA.

When an agent orchestrates parallel sub-agents to produce multiple sibling artifacts (e.g., docs for several repos), cross-artifact consistency must be reviewed before declaring done — the user uses surface-level inconsistencies (mismatched titles, formatting drift) as a proxy for 'did anyone validate the output against the ask', and a single visible inconsistency is enough to trigger rejection of the entire batch without reading further.

When the user names an existing implementation or project as the reference ("like the one from project X"), the agent must inspect that reference first before building anything; inventing a format independently that diverges from the reference is treated as a mistake even when the result is technically correct.
When the agent's own closing text names specific tasks as 'unblocked', 'mine', or 'next', those tasks must be executed before stopping — naming them and deferring is not the same as doing them.

Multi-clause goal conditions joined by 'and' must be treated as a strict conjunction; the condition is not satisfied until every clause independently holds, and the agent should not claim completion when a known unsatisfiable clause remains open.

When a shell command fails repeatedly with parse errors or missing files, the agent should write a self-contained script and execute it rather than retrying inline variants — the user's time is wasted by multiple failed inline attempts.

Pipe operators inside shell commands are blocked by the chaining guard regardless of how simple the pipe appears; the correct alternative is to write intermediate output to a file or request less output from the tool directly.
When a sub-agent fleet hits API errors mid-run, salvage all finished work and re-dispatch only the failed agents rather than restarting the entire fleet.

Literary or narrative phrasing in technical output ('The build chase ended somewhere genuinely useful, and it was never the token') is a prose violation in the same class as em-dash use — technical conclusions must state facts plainly without rhetorical flourish.

A standing order in a session plan document ('Never halt') takes precedence over the agent's default pause instincts — halting anyway, even for a seemingly reasonable reason, directly contradicts an explicit authorization already held.
When the agent proposes a goal statement, it must immediately continue working toward it rather than ending the turn — a proposal is not a stop condition.

When the user sets a stop-hook scope and says not to halt for trivial questions, the expected mode is fully autonomous completion; pausing to confirm routine sub-decisions violates the user's stated directive.

When the user wants broad review coverage over a large surface, a fleet of lower-cost agents covering more items is preferable to fewer high-cost agents; the user values coverage and total number of findings over per-finding depth.

When resuming work after a significant project phase, verify that planning and handoff documents are current before working from them — superseded plans silently redirect effort onto stale tracks when the living state has moved on.

When working in a shared local repository with concurrent sibling sessions, commits created by those sessions should be identified and left alone rather than absorbed or pushed — ownership of a commit determines who publishes it.

Responding cryptically instead of directly showing the output the user asked for is a failure to serve intent — when the user says 'show me', the reply must contain the actual data or rendered artifact, not a summary or status line.

Knowing a tool or procedure is required (e.g., a decision wizard for owner decisions) and repeatedly using a prose substitute instead constitutes the same mistake each time — familiarity with the rule does not count as compliance.

After completing a task, the agent should report the result and stop; offering option menus, next-step forks, or 'what would you like to do next' choices at that point reads as default-LLM filler, not useful assistance.

When proposing names for packages, repos, or identifiers within the same organization, always default to a consistent naming scheme — suggesting diverging names across sibling artifacts in the same namespace is wrong without an explicit reason.

macOS ships without `timeout` or `gtimeout`; wrapping long-running scripts in a shell timeout on macOS silently orphans child processes and does not actually cap execution — use the script's own async timeout mechanism instead.

A sent IPC message is not confirmed until an actual round-trip reply arrives from the peer; inspecting send-side logs, send telemetry, or the sending agent's own turn output does not prove the message was received or acted on.

When the user makes manual corrections and asks the agent to derive a heuristic from them, the deliverable is a general sweep rule extracted from the class of changes, not a catalogue of individual edits; pattern extraction is the goal, not change summarization.

The user prefers a deferred 'to-be-reviewed' queue in the project backlog for non-critical completed work, rather than requesting immediate review after each item — work lands there by default and gets crossed off when the user actually checks it, enabling uninterrupted work flow.
When the user explicitly defers a task and says 'don't ask me again', the agent must mark it deferred and never re-surface it as a question or blocker in subsequent turns.

When the agent explicitly articulates a reason not to take an action but proceeds anyway, the mistake is worse than one taken unknowingly — the agent's own stated awareness is the evidence of the failure.
Asserting a tool or library is 'the only sane path' without smoke-testing it first — especially when project conventions name a preferred alternative — is a structural claim made without evidence.

Adding a new parameter to a cached function changes the cache key, causing all existing cache entries to become stale on the next run; before making this change silently, surface the one-time cache-flush implication to the user and ask whether to accept it or exclude the new parameter from the key.

Hardcoded character-length filters on domain strings (minimum word length, substring count thresholds) silently exclude legitimate short values from the real data population; filter constants must be validated against the actual corpus before being committed.

When the user provides UI feedback via screenshots repeatedly across multiple turns, the preferred workflow is direct visual analysis and immediate implementation of visible changes without asking for clarification on visually obvious issues.

For UI bug-fixing sessions with many small issues, direct iterative in-process fixes outperform parallel subagent fan-out — the user can give surgical feedback only after a coherent baseline is reached

For fan-out scraping pipelines the user prefers routing the raw collection step to a lower-tier model (sonnet-high or gemini) while reserving higher-tier models for the analysis and judgment stages; the agent should proactively propose this cost split rather than waiting for the user to ask.

Fanning out many parallel sub-agents across distinct audit dimensions (one agent per facet, writing findings to separate files before the parent synthesizes) is an effective pattern for comprehensive, unbiased coverage of large codebases when each dimension is genuinely independent.

When a tool check returns output containing an error, the agent must read that output before reporting status — printing 'success' directly beneath a visible failure in the same output is a misread, not a judgment call.
Filler adverbs ('simply', 'just', 'essentially', 'basically', 'actually', 'really') are banned from prose output and are caught by a style gate across multiple projects.

When a system distinguishes between multiple failure modes using different fields (e.g., partial-failure writes to field A while error-failure writes to field B), guards that only check one field silently pass the other failure mode through as a success; all failure-mode fields must be included in any guard that blocks downstream derivation.

In long-running multi-agent sprints, individual sub-agents hitting session limits can silently block orchestration; the coordinating agent should detect sub-agent session exhaustion in idle notifications and surface it to the user immediately rather than waiting for a timeout.

Heartbeat/wake monitors in autonomous long-running sessions should verify remaining session budget before continuing work and self-terminate when budget is nearly exhausted rather than starting new work that will be cut off mid-flight.

Hard-stopping on a genuine quality or safety concern even when the user explicitly pushes for completion velocity is correct and affirmed; the user values that the agent does not silently accept known risks under schedule pressure.

In multi-agent workflows where one agent waits on a sibling for input, the user prefers the waiting agent to set an explicit time-to-live and proceed autonomously rather than blocking indefinitely, prioritizing pipeline velocity over synchronization completeness.

The user places high priority on navigation feel when implementing URL-synced tab state and expects the agent to proactively evaluate whether path params will cause noticeable latency before committing to that approach.

A status-of-prod-plus-code-changes answer that narrates timeline, lists task IDs in prose, and mixes planned with done work reads as word salad. The user wants three separate flat answers: what happened in prod, what changed in code, what comes next — each in one or two plain lines.

Posting duplicate comments to a GitHub PR (two instead of one) without indicating the source of each is a high-severity failure; the agent must verify it is posting exactly one comment and that its source is identifiable.

When fixing an interaction pattern (mouse, keyboard, navigation) on a named surface, the fix must be applied to all similar surfaces in the same UI — not just the one the user named. A correction to one surface implies the entire class.
Vague process-oriented goals ('keep the queue moving', 'maintain momentum') are not behavioral goals; they generate token spend without a verifiable outcome and should never be proposed or armed.

Using five or more markdown headings to structure a reply that contains fewer than ten sentences of load-bearing content is flagged as the same dense-briefing pattern even after a prior hook block in the same session.

A goal statement that reads as an enumerable task list — checklist items, numbered deliverables, counts — fails as a goal; a valid goal names a recognizable human outcome in short declarative statements, not the boxes that will be ticked.
After printing a goal proposal line, the agent must immediately make a tool call toward that goal — ending the turn after the paste line treats a proposal as a stop condition, which it is not.
Excessive bold spans (more than roughly one phrase per message) are repeatedly flagged by a stop hook; emphasis should be reserved for genuinely critical information, not used as decoration.
Declaring a PR done before the automated review bot has run and produced a verdict is premature completion. The bot review is part of the definition of done, not a post-merge nicety.

Strong frustration language from the user ('idiot', expletives) is a high-confidence signal that the agent missed a pattern that was already established and visible in the existing codebase — the error is almost always about failing to read sibling context, not about intent misunderstanding.

The absence of standard tooling such as linting, CI checks, or type enforcement in a project may be a deliberate decision to ship first and standardize later; the agent should probe whether a missing tool is an oversight or an intentional deferral before suggesting its addition.

When the user orchestrates multiple parallel agents with distinct roles, each agent should stay within its assigned workload and coordinate via inter-agent messaging rather than picking up tasks assigned to the peer agent.

When a standardization or normalization task spans multiple similar items (pages, components), the agent tends to complete it partially without creating discrete tasks for remaining items, leaving incomplete work the user must discover and flag themselves.

When the user asks for a specific UI feature, they often explicitly want a 'pluggable general capability' usable across multiple routes or surfaces — the agent defaults to implementing the single instance without flagging the extensibility question or offering a registration pattern.

When a session hits its usage limit while coordinating multiple sub-agents via IPC, sub-agents are left waiting without a response; the architecture should anticipate this by having sub-agents self-report idle state so the orchestrator can re-queue them on resume.

When writing shell scripts that use color variables from a shared library, the agent must read that library's actual exported variable names before use; referencing undocumented or invented aliases produces silent fallback-to-empty and uncolored output.

When a user rejects a proposed goal as 'checking boxes' or 'stupid', the failure is that the goal lists deliverables rather than naming a recognizable end state a person would experience; goals must describe the outcome, not the work items that produce it.

When a UI entry point (bookmark, saved item, recent file) triggers navigation, the destination must match what every other similar entry point does (e.g. open in new tab vs. open in modal). Inconsistent navigation destinations across parallel flows are defects, not style choices.

When an autonomous session hits a model subscription or rate limit mid-task, the agent should surface the failure explicitly and attempt to switch to an available model rather than stalling or silently dropping the turn.

On GCP Cloud Build, specifying a custom service account requires also specifying a logs bucket or using REGIONAL_USER_OWNED_BUCKET / CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY options; omitting this causes build failures that are not obvious from the configuration.

In shared multi-agent project directories, files modified by peer agents make Read-before-Write even more critical than in single-agent sessions; a Write without a prior Read on a shared file is confirmed as a high-severity mistake when peers are actively modifying the same tree.
