An idle notification from a sub-agent that was already stopped earlier in the session is stale and should not trigger any action; the agent should recognize it as a no-op rather than re-routing work.

When a task or standing ruling specifies exactly which model tier to use for sub-agent seats (e.g., 'one fable planning seat'), dispatching sub-agents at a different tier violates that ruling even if the agent has read it in the same turn.
A CSS custom property declared as empty (`--x: ;`) is not a default: `var(--x, fallback)` substitutes the empty value rather than the fallback. Omit the declaration entirely to let the fallback fire.
A CSS registered property with `inherits: false` is invisible to `::before`, `::after`, and child elements; any property intended for pseudo-elements must not use `inherits: false`.

An agent that builds a linting or validation tool and then ships output without running that tool on its own output has failed the exercise-based verification rule; the tool's existence does not count as having used it.

When the agent claims to have exhausted a set of options ('every X I tried'), but the actual tool invocation history shows fewer attempts than the claim implies, the claim is false and misleads the user about the search space.
A rule or protocol scoped to a specific condition (e.g., 'during owner absence') must not be applied when that condition is not met; the scope clause is a precondition, not decoration.

When the user says 'do not pick stupid fields' or similar judgment constraints, the agent must apply genuine editorial judgment — only surfacing fields with clear user value — rather than enumerating every technically-editable field.

When a sub-agent hits a credential or authentication block outside its own scope, surfacing the exact command the user must run and then holding (not attempting workarounds) unblocks the human in one action.

When designing a new UI component variant or layout, the agent proceeds directly to implementation without showing the user a visual mock or sample first, losing the opportunity for early feedback before code is written.

A UI review or verification performed only in one theme state (dark or light) is a partial verification; findings should be scoped to what was actually exercised rather than presented as a complete audit.

When implementing a shared UI shell component (sidebar, drawer, modal), the agent must audit ALL pages in the application for the same component before writing any code — implementing per-page variants of a globally-shared shell requires a costly full-app refactor to fix and is a recurring systematic miss.

UI review reports generated by testing in only one visual mode (e.g., dark mode only) produce false positives that waste the user's triage time; review findings should be annotated with which mode was observed, or the review should cover both modes before reporting.

List pages missing pagination when sibling list pages in the same codebase already implement it should be flagged and fixed proactively — treating each list page in isolation when the pattern is proven nearby is a systematic miss.

When a file path appears at or near the end of a sentence in a reply, placing a period immediately after the path (inside or outside backticks) breaks terminal hyperlinking; always follow a path with a space, a word, or a comma before any punctuation.
Status update responses that are dense and verbose ('word salad') are rejected; the user wants concise, actionable, state-first output, not a narrated stream of what was done.

When an agent documents a UI gesture (rename, drag, click) as working without having driven it in a real browser, the documentation is fabricated — 'confirmed' claims about interactive behaviors require browser exercise, not code inspection.
Replies that lead with a narration of actions taken rather than the decision or result are a standing failure mode; the first line must be the one thing the user must decide or act on.

Publishing content to an external hosted service requires an explicit ask from the user in the current conversation; local tooling (kanban server, decision pages) is always preferred for visual review
When a task is complete the agent should report status and stop; option menus and forks should only appear at genuine decision points, not as a default closing move

When the user establishes an explicit deferred-review queue for completed non-critical work, route finished items there automatically rather than interrupting flow to seek immediate review confirmation after each task.
When setting up deployment pipelines for autonomous sessions, the user prefers fully async flows that do not block the agent waiting for interactive authentication steps such as browser-based OAuth.

The agent reads diagnostic output (e.g., a failure message or a status section) that names the exact root cause, then attributes the failure to a different cause, ignoring the evidence already in hand.
After a long-running feature branch completes its work, the agent should proactively flag that the branch has not been merged to main rather than leaving the user to notice it themselves.

When the user's UI feedback describes multiple overlapping issues with a component (spacing, width, card layout, field arrangement), the agent should enumerate its planned changes against ALL the named issues before implementing, rather than acting on a subset.

A sidebar or drawer that appears on multiple pages is a candidate for a single shared shell component; the agent should check for sibling usages before writing a page-local implementation and flag divergence proactively.

When an IPC peer agent misses a reply-by deadline, the orchestrating session should detect the timeout via inbox check and proceed on available work rather than stalling — non-response is a recoverable state, not a blocker.

Spawning an independent adversarial validation sub-agent to produce a structured PASS/FAIL verdict before committing to a design is a reliable gate pattern — the validator's explicit verdict ('PASS-WITH-NOTES') gives the orchestrator a clear signal to act on.
When the user asks for a tracking artifact for their own reference, provide a human-facing doc they can independently consult, separate from any agent-internal state or memory files.

When the agent proposes a goal statement and ends the turn immediately, it violates the intent of the rule: the proposal is not a stop — the agent must immediately continue working toward the stated goal unless blocked on information only the user holds.

A reply that opens with a summary of a file just written in the same turn restates content the user can already see and buries the actual news; the reply should lead with the one thing the user needs to act on.

When fixing a UI interaction bug (click behavior, keyboard shortcuts, navigation), the fix must be applied to every similar surface in the application, not just the one the user named — surfaces like sidebars, path bars, and tab strips have the same contract and a partial fix will be called out as incomplete.

Self-grading done-claim openers ('Done. Here's where your answers landed.') are flagged; the done verdict belongs to the user, and the agent should lead with what is factually true rather than declaring success.
Declaring an e2e suite 'confirmed' from one isolated probe before running the full suite (both themes, all smoke paths) is a premature-done error; the stated gate must be the gate exercised.
Declaring a feature done based on code being ready or an API call succeeding is insufficient; done means the full user-facing flow is exercised end-to-end including deploy, migrations, and UI.
When the user asks for a minimal patchy fix, the agent must not propose new infrastructure or meta-state mechanisms (locks, queues, dedicated services) even if they would be more correct.

When a goal condition lists specific scenarios that must be screenshotted and recorded, the agent must not attempt to satisfy the condition with partial evidence; each listed scenario must be independently exercised and evidenced.

When a sub-agent sends a duplicate idle notification after already delivering its findings and being stopped, the correct response is to recognize it as a stale echo and take no action — re-processing or re-querying would be wasted work.

Before invoking an expensive adversarial or multi-agent review, update the spec or artifact being reviewed to reflect current reality; running a costly review against a stale spec wastes tokens and produces misleading findings.

When the user forcefully denies a structural claim the agent made (calling it a lie or demanding a recon), the correct response is to reread the actual artifacts and report literal state — not to fold the correction into a new narrative or capitulate with softer wording.

When the user wants resource or capacity limits enforced, they prefer policy doctrine (a written ladder with per-band actions) over hard-coded mechanical checks, because policies are flexible and don't require code changes when thresholds shift.
Agent planning notes and inline commentary left in committed code should be stripped before a PR is raised; the user explicitly removes them as noise in the diff.

When a blocker requires user action to unblock (e.g., credentials, environment access), the agent must surface the exact blocker with a clear actionable ask in the same turn rather than silently waiting across multiple goal check-in cycles.

Background automation (pm2 services, cron jobs, warm-up processes) that the user explicitly rejected or never requested must not reappear in later turns as suggestions or implicit parts of a broader plan; an explicit 'don't want this' is a hard stop for that surface, not a soft preference to weigh.

When the agent authors a new constraint rule (e.g., a style ban, a UI invariant) in documentation within a session, it can immediately violate that same constraint in output produced later in the same session — writing the rule does not auto-apply it to concurrent in-flight work.

The agent must verify authentication and preconditions with a cheap smoke test before triggering long-running or expensive operations (e.g., multi-part e2e runs); skipping this check when the user expects it is an explicit correction trigger.

When the agent produces a dense or poorly structured output containing correct information, the user expects restructuring without any information loss; 'word salad' is a structural failure, not a content failure, and the fix is better structure, not a summary.

Shipping a UI component as complete when it reads as visually sparse or information-poor triggers strong user correction; visual completeness and density must be verified alongside code correctness before marking a UI task done.

A polished self-critical reply (numbered RCA, formatted pattern list, structured acknowledgment) reads as covering tracks rather than correcting behavior; the user rejects performative self-criticism and expects a changed method, not a well-formatted acknowledgment.

For evaluating new tooling or models against an established suite, the user applies a two-tier scrutiny rule: proven use cases already in the suite need no re-evaluation, but new promises require active testing and a higher justification threshold before adoption.

A keyboard shortcut that the user has been told opens a panel or modal must be wired to that UI element as a baseline requirement. Shipping the modal without the keybinding is an incomplete implementation, not a later enhancement.
When the user asks for a visual or design ruling, the agent must produce a rendered mockup or screenshot, not a hex-code plan or text spec with a 'recommended' framing

When presenting an architectural ambiguity or tradeoff decision to the user, lead with a one-sentence plain-English framing of the choice, concrete codebase examples of each option, and the specific tradeoffs — never present the problem in abstract technical terms without grounding

A checkpoint directive that was correct when written can become incorrect or harmful by the time a subsequent session reads it, because the codebase changes between sessions — treat checkpoint instructions as snapshots of intent, not standing orders, and re-verify before applying them.

Before claiming deployed URLs or documentation links are working, the agent should fetch them over HTTP and read the response; code-level correctness does not substitute for live endpoint verification.

Showing a task list from the wrong session context is actively worse than not showing one; the user reacts with strong frustration, suggesting the agent must verify list scope against the current session before presenting it

When the user establishes graduated thresholds (e.g. soft warn / prune signal / hard blocker) for a resource limit, they prefer the ladder be enforced as documented policy rather than hardcoded numeric checks, so the policy can be adjusted without a code change.
Adding browser/DOM dependencies to unit tests is rejected; unit tests must remain lightweight and headless.

When a prior PR's title deliberately omitted a marker (e.g. [nobot]), the agent should treat that as a project-level convention change and not restore the marker on subsequent PRs in the same repository.
Prose must avoid em-dashes entirely (budget is zero) and minimize bold emphasis (near one phrase per message); violating either is a style error requiring correction

Style-ledger enforcement (prose smell, thesaurus checks) works well as a fleet of isolated single-turn sub-sessions rather than inline work — each session receives the text on stdin, applies a scoped ledger, and returns violations without polluting the main context.
When the agent raises a PR, it must verify the PR has no merge conflicts before reporting it as ready for review or merge.
The agent must not re-add PR title flags (e.g., [nobot], [noslack]) that the user had intentionally removed.
The agent must not write output with em-dashes, excessive bold spans, or option menus when the task is already determined; plain declarative prose with meaning-first ordering is required.
When deferring an atone invocation to a later turn, the agent compounds the mistake; atone must be invoked in the same turn the error is identified.

A sub-agent 'voice pass' over a PR description is insufficient to remove AI-smell if the pass only lints surface prose; it must also strip verdict labels ('Verdict: Ready for release'), accusatory framing ('not verified by hand'), obsolete steps, and non-intuitive opening structures.

PR description review contracts that call out unverified items using phrases like 'not verified by hand' read as accusatory to the user; the section should plainly name what was tested and what scripts or steps cover it, with no blame framing.

Using generic role labels like 'runner' or 'console' in shared docs instead of explicit product/project names is a documentation defect the user will catch and correct; always use the unambiguous qualified name.

When the user has previously deferred work on a specific artifact or app unless a concrete trigger condition is met (e.g., customer demand), do not surface that work again in recommendations unless the trigger condition has been explicitly confirmed in the current session.

When asked to interact with a UI wizard or form, the agent must drive the actual interface rather than fabricate field values from assumptions — invented field values (vocabulary, column names) bypass the real system and produce wrong results.

The user's definition of 'all surfaces' for testing includes visual correctness, full happy-path functionality with no errors, informational disclosure, and absence of false owner-gate flags — not just API-level checks.

Declaring documentation or web-served pages 'done' without performing an actual HTTP fetch to verify they are reachable and render correctly is treated by the user as a critical verification failure, not a minor omission.

A UI layout change involving tables or wide content must be verified by actually opening the page in a browser at desktop width before shipping; no parity ledger entry for a table's rendered width means no width constraint was checked.

When an agent queries a data structure or inbox for metadata fields only (e.g. sender, alias, timestamp), then describes or makes claims about the content of those items without reading the body or payload, the claim is structurally wrong — projecting a subset of fields and asserting the whole.

When the agent's own reasoning identifies the correct next action, stopping to ask the user to confirm that same action before executing it is unnecessary and frustrating — identify-then-execute, not identify-then-ask.

Technical planning documents intended for human skimming require visual hierarchy by default: tables, JSON payload shape examples, and ASCII architectural diagrams — prose-only documents fail the scan test regardless of factual accuracy.

When the user requests a plan document, producing a published artifact or shareable output beyond the doc is unsolicited scope expansion — plan docs stay internal unless the user explicitly asks to publish.

Before handing shell commands or regex patterns to the user for manual execution, the agent should test the command against a trivial known input to verify correctness — skipping this step after explicitly acknowledging it would be helpful is a clear failure.

When a project document the agent has explicitly read contains behavioral directives, acting against those directives immediately afterward is a higher-severity failure than acting without having read them.

When synthesizing findings from multiple sub-agents that each audited different projects, the agent must verify it is writing the synthesis for the project the user asked about, not the project the sub-agents happened to be running in. A cross-project multi-seat research flow is especially susceptible to this scope drift.

When the user has explicitly granted an authorization (push to main, use a tool, proceed with a plan), the agent repeatedly halting to seek the same permission again costs goodwill and blocks progress; treat an explicit grant as standing until explicitly revoked.

When writing documentation intended for handoff to a new collaborator, the agent must strip all internal shorthand, session-contextual references, and assumed-shared vocabulary — every noun gets its full project-qualified name.
Printing a /goal paste line and stopping is a halt on authority already held; the agent must begin the first tool call toward that goal in the same turn.

Excessive bold spans (>10 per reply) and 'not-X-but-Y' contrast scaffolding are detectable LLM-register tells that fire the prose-smell gate; plain meaning-first sentences without decorative emphasis are the correct register.

Sub-agent dispatch prompts must never instruct the sub-agent to write a file literally named `report.md`; the harness blocks this write, causing the sub-agent to either fail or fall back to inline return, which may not be persisted. Use descriptive, non-generic filenames in output paths.

Sub-agent dispatch prompts must include an explicit spend ceiling or budget constraint clause; omitting it while including other constraint clauses is a recognized failure even when the other clauses are present.

UI variant distinctness must be verified by reading rendered output (screenshots, browser), not by comparing markup strings, element counts, or diff size — the user evaluates what they see, not what the diff says.

When the user has already supplied specific corrective feedback and explicit authorization to proceed, the agent must execute the fix directly rather than initiating another review or audit cycle — a redundant audit substitutes for action and is a halt on authority already held.

When building a utility tool meant to simplify an existing workflow, the agent over-engineered the solution relative to comparable free alternatives; the user explicitly prioritized simplicity and immediate usability over technical sophistication.
Publishing a rendered HTML artifact when a plain markdown file would serve the purpose is an over-engineering error; and any HTML output that is published must include a light/dark mode toggle.

A decision surface that costs the owner more time and tokens than direct chat answers is worse than not building it; the measure of a decision UI is whether it reduces owner effort, not whether it exists.

Claiming a file or path does not exist based on a grep that respects .gitignore or skips hidden files is an invalid absence claim; only an ignore-transparent search (rg --no-ignore --hidden, test -f, or stat) can establish actual absence.
When a simple one-command verification step exists (e.g., a liveness filter, a last-commit check), the agent should run it before using an unfiltered count or raw list as a load-bearing argument.

When the user asks for a summary or TL;DR of documents, provide key insights, decisions, and important nuances structured in points/subsections/tables — not a quality assessment or grading of the docs' content

Claiming code is 'deployed' or 'live' without observing the actual behavior in the live environment (log line, real output, visible effect) fails the declared-ready bar; deployment is not proof of behavior.

Route-critical, non-secret identifiers (team IDs, entity slugs) belong in the URL as path or query params, not hidden in client state — this enables deep linking, sharing, and browser-native navigation.

Planning and architectural documents must name real problems, unknown unknowns, and counter-arguments to proposed solutions — enterprise jargon that dresses up avoidance of hard questions is not acceptable

When asked to use an existing skill or integration for a task, the agent should first verify the skill has sufficient capabilities for the specific task rather than attempting to execute and discovering gaps mid-execution.

When generating automated CI comments or bot output, the agent must render and read the output as a human reviewer would before posting; machine tokens (raw enum codes, internal identifiers) leaking into human-facing output is a shipping defect, not a cosmetic issue.

CI or bot prose that explains its own purpose meta-narratively ('A nose, not a gate: nothing here blocks anything') is itself AI-smell; the output format should demonstrate its intent by its structure, not announce it in filler sentences.

Workflow sub-agents dispatched by a harness that blocks their Write tool must return findings as text; the parent agent is responsible for persisting them to disk — the sub-agent cannot write directly.
The user prefers completed, non-critical work to be queued in an async 'to be reviewed' list rather than prompting an immediate review — only critical items warrant blocking for user attention.

When the user explicitly defines domain terminology (role names, status labels, naming conventions), write the definitions to a canonical reference document immediately rather than keeping them in conversation context only — named terminology that is not recorded will drift across sessions.

When an agent poses an explicit either/or question and the user responds with a bare affirmative ('yes', 'ok'), the agent must not silently pick whichever branch is already in motion; the ambiguous response resolves neither branch and requires a one-line disambiguation before acting.
A repair or generalization that was valid for one artifact is incorrectly applied to a second, unrelated artifact with different characteristics, producing a worse outcome than taking no action.

The agent reads its own session-start checklist output that explicitly flags a required action (e.g., 'ARM YOUR HEARTBEAT', a named plan-of-record path) but then proceeds without taking that action, treating the checklist as read-only rather than directive.

When a Stop hook fires because remaining tasks are genuinely blocked on owner decisions, the agent should enumerate the specific blocked items once, state nothing more can close from its side, and hold — not repeat the same state description across multiple turns.
When the agent is blocked on a sub-task and other tasks remain open, it must proceed with the open tasks and escalate the blocker once rather than reporting blocked and halting.

Once a navigational or architectural pattern is established (e.g., placing route-critical identifiers in URL path or query params), the user expects it applied consistently across all surfaces — partial adoption that applies it in some pages but not others draws explicit correction.

When the agent raises concerns about a blocked state (e.g. hardware unreachable), it should verify current state first before escalating or 'throwing a fuss'; the user invoked /atone for this pattern explicitly.

When an agent implements a domain model without questioning whether the model makes business sense (e.g., a billing unit with no clear divisibility), the user must catch the flaw themselves; the agent should surface the inconsistency proactively before building, not after.
Do not re-run reviews or validation passes mid-task when there are still incomplete implementation tasks; finish all tasks first, then address review findings section by section

Acknowledging a routing or structural pattern in one place but implementing a workaround elsewhere (e.g., dropdown instead of path param for the same semantic concept) is treated as an inconsistency failure, not a judgment call.

Route-critical, non-secret identifiers (team IDs, entity slugs) belong in the URL as path or query params rather than in client state or dropdowns — the user frames this as a 'robust' practice that unlocks deep-linking and shareable URLs.

When implementing a runtime config or feature-flag system, the user expects both a storage/retrieval mechanism and a frontend admin UI for editing values as part of the same deliverable — not as a follow-up phase.
When pivoting away from partially-staged changes mid-session, the user prefers parking them via git stash rather than committing or discarding them, preserving the work for potential resumption.

Commit messages and PR descriptions must be concise and human-sounding; the user explicitly audits these artifacts with a style review tool and treats AI-prose register in commits as a defect on par with code issues.

When verifying a third-party service integration (logging, analytics, monitoring), the primary evidence target is the vendor's own dashboard — not an internal admin tab or agent-built view, which may succeed in isolation while the real integration is broken.
UI-side logging must be structural-event-only and must never include personally identifiable information; this is a hard constraint, not a default that can be relaxed per feature.

Multi-level agent fan-out for review or reporting skills is over-engineering when a simpler, single-pass approach produces the same output; prefer the simpler path unless the task is genuinely parallel.

A skill or sub-agent tasked with critiquing a particular output defect can produce output that suffers from the same defect it was meant to catch; verify the critic's own output format before treating its findings as authoritative.
When the user asks for an optional component to be 'separate and independent,' they mean architecturally decoupled — disabling or breaking one component must not degrade the other.

A background system whose effects are invisible to the user — even when it is working correctly and producing measurable traces — will fail to feel useful; background learning or automation systems need explicit, surface-visible feedback loops.

When the user asks to be 'shown' a document or artifact, the agent must surface the artifact itself — not a prose summary of its contents. A summary of what is in a doc is not the same as showing the doc.

Feature toggles and runtime flags should not be placed in backend environment config when the user has indicated they want a separate runtime config system; env config and runtime config are distinct systems with fundamentally different change mechanisms.

When the user explicitly calls out an output format as bad, the correction applies to the entire class of that format (pipe-delimited dumps, wire-format leaks) — not just the one instance named; fix the format class, not the specimen.

When a skill or tool is only relevant to one specific project or context, it should live as a project-local skill rather than a global one; the agent should not make project-specific tooling available globally.

When the agent offers a goal line at session start for a clearly scoped, mechanical continuation task, the user finds it friction-adding and rejects it; goal proposals should be suppressed when the task is a direct continuation with an obvious, bounded outcome.
After a session catchup, the agent emitted a verbose status briefing instead of immediately resuming work; the user expects action, not a summary of state they already know.

Claiming a UI change is done without actually running the changed path and reading the rendered output triggers a hook correction; only a live browser exercise with a screenshot read counts as verification.

When the agent emits a multi-paragraph status update listing what it did rather than leading with the one thing the user must decide or do, the user asks for a simpler summary; the first line should be the single actionable fact.

For review and audit reports, the user prefers grouping findings by logical domain or category rather than by severity; severity should be surfaced only as a label when high, not as the primary organizing axis.

When an output format or report structure has been refined through meta-review (e.g., applying /skeptical-review to a review report), the user expects the improvements to be codified back into the reusable skill template, not applied only to the one-off instance.

When infrastructure components (monitors, IPC handlers) can serve multiple purposes without added complexity, the user prefers consolidation over adding dedicated single-purpose components, citing session monitor budget constraints.
When context or time is limited, the user accepts proceeding with non-irreversible foundational changes and deferring context-dependent decisions to a follow-up session rather than blocking entirely.
When a sub-agent finishes and sends an idle notification, the agent should verify the output file actually exists before reading findings from it rather than trusting the notification summary.

When dispatching a sub-agent to audit feature completeness or capability gaps, the agent must verify which document is the authoritative user-authored source before dispatching — not a downstream AI-generated derived artifact. Reviewing gaps against a derived doc instead of the originating spec produces systematically wrong verdicts.

When the user cannot open local file paths (e.g., in a terminal context), the agent must inline the content or provide a fully qualified accessible URL — linking to a local artifact is not a fallback.
Glossary entries and terminology tables for a domain document should distinguish between domain-specific data/functional concepts and general terminology in separate tables, not mix them.

An adversarial review mode should operate from an active hostile starting premise — that the main agent made fundamental errors — rather than a balanced skeptical stance; it should seek out untested paths and produce evidence of failure, not merely raise concerns.

In high-throughput sessions where the user cannot review each completed item immediately, maintaining a named staging queue (e.g., 'to-be-reviewed') for completed non-critical work allows the user to batch-verify at their own pace rather than being interrupted for review after each task.

When writing a session checkpoint or core-dump during work driven by multiple simultaneous sources (user requests, sub-agent adversarial reviews, product specs), each task entry must explicitly label its driving authority; omitting this forces the next session to re-derive which items came from which source and risks attributing adversarial-review-driven work as user-directed work.

Under cognitive load from multi-task autonomous sessions, the agent defaults to a dense, reference-heavy communication register ('cryptic') instead of plain direct speech, requiring explicit correction.

Heartbeat or resume payloads that embed live state readings (counts, SHA hashes, gate lists, diagnoses) go stale within hours and cause subsequent sessions to act on incorrect state; heartbeat payloads should instruct the recipient to recompute all state from live instruments rather than trusting embedded values.

Decision-gate verification requires cross-checking the rendered output against all standing constraints and prior rulings in the same turn before displaying it; an agent that reads constraints for other purposes in the same turn but does not apply them to the gate output has still failed the check.
The agent repeatedly claims a change is done or working without exercising the changed code path in the same turn; stop hooks and the juror both confirm this as a real mistake, not a false positive

When a feature is explicitly scoped to a narrow use case (e.g., only one template type or region), implement it with hardcoded explicit conditions rather than runtime self-gating logic that could be silently bypassed or broadened by future callers.

Product-level decisions embedded in implementation (e.g., which items enter a review queue, which workflow stages apply to a feature) are owner decisions that must be flagged explicitly for user sign-off rather than resolved silently by the agent as implementation details.

When the user explicitly signals deadline pressure and asks the agent to proceed autonomously on reversible work without their context, the agent should proceed without waiting for missing clarifications.

When a bug repro is confirmed to be narrower than originally described (e.g., triggers in one entry point but not another), collecting that discriminating detail before starting the fix substantially reduces the risk of patching the wrong code path.
Claiming to have fixed a UI or runtime bug without actually exercising the fix on the running dev server leads to repeated false assurance cycles that damage trust.
When the user asks a direct question mid-stream, the agent must answer that question before continuing other work; proceeding without answering reads as ignoring the user.
Agent-authored documentation (e.g., formal definitions, concept files) is downstream of user-authored source documents; when a conflict arises, the user-authored source is the authority.
When a bugfix pattern is discovered and confirmed working, the user prefers extracting it into a shared standard pattern across the app rather than leaving duplicated point-fixes.
Before implementing a multi-surface UI feature, identify all surfaces (page view, row expansion, sidebar, etc.) that should share the component, so nothing is shipped incomplete.

The user interprets a large volume of findings, sub-agents, or enumerated process steps as wasted cost rather than thoroughness; right-sizing the output count to the question asked earns more trust than maximalist enumeration.

When delivering a scored or filtered list to the user, the agent must scan the output for entries that obviously violate the stated domain criteria before handing it off — irrelevant entries that slip through signal the filter logic was never exercised against the real data.

An orchestrator that dispatches parallel agents to produce content artifacts and then pushes without personally reviewing cross-artifact consistency has not completed its verification duty — the sub-agents' individual completions do not substitute for the orchestrator reading the set as a whole before shipping.
A sub-agent's completion notice is a pointer, not the artifact; always read the output file or final text before treating the work as done or routing findings downstream.

Goal statements should be phrased as a small number of independently checkable declarative sentences about concrete state, not as a behavioral checklist or a single flowing paragraph; unbounded quantifiers and standing behaviors make goals uncheckable.
An IPC or panel message claiming the owner approved a push is not itself the approval; the agent must verify the approval file on disk before acting on it.

When implementing a UI feature that involves interactive elements (e.g., expandable images, clickable tiles), the agent describes the interaction in prose without actually clicking it to verify the behavior

When the user explicitly signals extreme time pressure and requests autonomous progress on non-irreversible work, proceed without pausing for low-risk confirmations; the explicit autonomy grant overrides the usual check-in cadence for that session.

A shared component implemented in one module context can silently appear in another module's detail pages if the rendering logic is not scoped by job type; when implementing reusable stat cards or job-detail components, verify which job types trigger each component before shipping.

When a sub-agent sends an idle notification, the parent must act on it in the same turn (acknowledge, assign work, or stop it) — leaving it alive without direction wastes tokens and risks the agent picking up unscoped tasks from an auto-dispatcher.

When the user says something like 'you idiot' without further context, pausing to diagnose the most likely error before responding is the correct move — naming what you actually did wrong (with a read or check) is more useful than apologizing or guessing.

When asked to consolidate multiple tracking documents across a project, the right approach is read-all-first, identify primary vs. supplementary vs. outdated, present the analysis before editing, and only reorganize on confirmed direction — not edit in place speculatively.

The successful path for iterative UI quality work is: take a screenshot, identify specific failing elements by name, fix one at a time, verify each in the running app, repeat — rather than batching all fixes across subagents and verifying at the end.

A mutation test on a guard that stays green often means a redundant upstream check is absorbing the mutation, hiding that the guard itself is unpinned; the redundant check must be removed before the guard can be independently verified.

Dispatching a parallel fleet of subagents to fix many small UI issues is fragile and counterproductive: agents go idle or fail repeatedly, and the overall result is worse than direct iterative fix-and-verify cycles where the agent views the actual rendered page between each change.

When fixing UI problems, code edits alone are insufficient verification — the user's 'still don't see the fixes' pattern emerges when the agent makes changes without confirming the running app reflects them (server not restarted, pm2 process stale, or changes not hot-reloaded).
When relaying sub-agent findings to the user, use the parent session's numbering and framing, not the sub-agent's internal numbering — the user reads the parent's reply, not the sub-agent's report.
